title: De quibusdam eximiis proprietatibus circa divisores potestatum occurrentibus

deep.reconstruction: This is the opening of E557 (Acta Acad. Sci. Petropolitanae 1778:II, printed 1783). §1 sets up the problem in modern terms. For gcd(a,N)=1 the residues of 1, a, a^2, ... mod N are purely periodic, because a is a unit mod N. So there is a least n with a^n ≡ 1 (mod N), the multiplicative order ord_N(a), and the residues repeat with period n. For prime N, Fermat's little theorem gives a^{N-1} ≡ 1, and when the order n is smaller than N-1 it divides N-1. Euler then asks for ord_N(a) for any given N. He generalises twice. First: find the least x with a^x ≡ r (mod N), i.e. the discrete logarithm or index. Second: find x with f·a^x + g ≡ 0 (mod N), i.e. a^x ≡ -g·f^{-1}. §2 gives the motivation, perfect numbers. Even perfect numbers have the form 2^{n-1}(2^n-1) with 2^n-1 prime, which forces n to be prime, since 2^{αβ}-1 is divisible by 2^α-1 and 2^β-1. The converse fails: n = 11, 23, 29, 37 give composite Mersenne numbers. Euler recalls his old sieve. Let a prime divisor be q = 2p+1. Then 2^{2p} ≡ 1 (mod q). Since 2^n ≡ 1 too and n is prime, ord_q(2) = n divides 2p. Hence every divisor has the form 2λn+1, and products of such numbers keep that form. The following page continues: Fermat's numbers 2^{2^m}+1, the factor 641 of 2^{32}+1, and the question of the least x with 641 | 2^x+1. It then announces a 'new, much simpler method' for the general index problem, built on Lemmas 1-5. These lemmas let one shift residues by multiples of N, multiply them, divide them, and cancel powers of a, a reduction/descent scheme for computing indices.
errors: The argument 'formula 2^{2p}-1 always has divisor 2p+1' assumes 2p+1 is prime (Fermat's little theorem). It is valid for prime divisors only; the conclusion for all divisors follows because products of numbers ≡1 mod 2n stay ≡1 mod 2n. Euler leaves this implicit.
Stating that 2^{αβ}-1 has divisors 2^α-1 and 2^β-1 is correct. The listed composite exponents 11, 23, 29, 37 are correct (factors 23, 47, 233, 223).

deep.surprise_reason: This page is an introduction restating well-known results: order of a residue, the Mersenne divisor form and the 641 factor. The algorithmic content (an index-computation method) begins on later pages and is known as part of E557.
transcription_corrections: Transcription is essentially accurate. On the next page, Lemma 3's 'A^{x+y}' should read a^{x+y} (printer's capital).
